# Apaṇṇaka Sutta (MN 60 (PTS MN i 400))

**ID:** MN 60 (PTS MN i 400)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Apaṇṇaka Sutta* ("The Incontrovertible Teaching" or "Unfailing") is the 60th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Delivered in a brāhman village to an audience of uncommitted householders, the discourse presents a rational reflection designed to help listeners navigate contentious religious doctrines [McTighe 2001; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Rather than presupposing the truth of rebirth and moral responsibility, the Buddha presents a pragmatic, wager-like argument reminiscent of Pascal's wager: even without immediate direct knowledge, adopting the view that actions bear moral fruit and that an afterlife exists is "unfailing" or safe, because it prevents harmful behavior in this life and protects against potential misfortune in the next [Berkwitz 2013; Flores 2008; Jayatilleke 1975; Anālayo 2018]. In doing so, the Buddha systematically refutes rival contemporary teachings such as nihilism (*natthikavāda*), non-action (*akiriyavāda*), and causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), warning that adhering to these doctrines fosters unwholesome states and leads to lower rebirths [Flores 2008; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anderson 1999]. The text also treats problematic views concerning the immaterial realms and embodies an early form of Buddhist doxographical analysis [Westerhoff 2018; Radich 2007].

DharmaNexus aligns the sutta's text-reuse units internally with numerous Pali discourses—most heavily with the *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), the *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), MN 94, MN 76, and DN 2—and identifies cross-language correspondences in the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu*, Tibetan Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises, and Chinese Āgama collections (*Madhyama-āgama* T 26 and *Ekottarika-āgama* T 125) [DharmaNexus].
